commands.name: cloudflare:agents-sdk
commands.description: (cloudflare) Build AI agents on Cloudflare Workers using the Agents SDK. Load when creating stateful agents, durable workflows, real-time WebSocket apps, scheduled tasks, MCP servers, chat applications, voice agents, or browser automation. commands.name: cloudflare:cloudflare
commands.description: (cloudflare) Comprehensive Cloudflare platform skill covering Workers, Pages, storage (KV, D1, R2), AI (Workers AI, Vectorize, Agents SDK), feature flags (Flagship), networking (Tunnel, Spectrum), security (WAF, DDoS), and infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, Pulumi). Use for any Cloudflare development task. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.

commands.name: cloudflare:cloudflare-email-service
commands.description: (cloudflare) Send and receive transactional emails with Cloudflare Email Service (Email Sending + Email Routing). Use when building email sending (Workers binding or REST API), email routing, Agents SDK email handling, or integrating email into any app — Workers, Node.js, Python, Go, etc. Also use for email deliverability, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, wrangler email setup, MCP email tools, or when a coding agent needs to send emails. Even for simple requests like "add email to my Worker" — this skill has critical config details.

commands.name: cloudflare:cloudflare-one

commands.name: cloudflare:sandbox-sdk

commands.name: cloudflare:turnstile-spin
commands.description: (cloudflare) Set up Cloudflare Turnstile end-to-end in a project. Scan the codebase, create the widget via the Cloudflare API, embed it where user requests need bot verification (form submissions, SPA actions, API endpoints, download links, comment or vote submissions, etc.), wire canonical server-side siteverify in the customer's existing backend, validate, and persist the skill. Load this when a user asks to add Turnstile, set up CAPTCHA, protect a form or endpoint from bots, or fix a Turnstile integration. Mirrors developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/spin.

commands.name: cloudflare:web-perf
commands.description: (cloudflare) Analyzes web performance using Chrome DevTools MCP. Measures Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) and supplementary metrics (FCP, TBT, Speed Index), identifies render-blocking resources, network dependency chains, layout shifts, caching issues, and accessibility gaps. Use when asked to audit, profile, debug, or optimize page load performance, Lighthouse scores, or site speed. Biases towards retrieval from current documentation over pre-trained knowledge.

commands.name: cloudflare:workers-best-practices
commands.description: (cloudflare) Reviews and authors Cloudflare Workers code against production best practices. Load when writing new Workers, reviewing Worker code, configuring wrangler.jsonc, or checking for common Workers anti-patterns (streaming, floating promises, global state, secrets, bindings, observability). Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.

commands.name: cloudflare:wrangler
commands.description: (cloudflare) Cloudflare Workers CLI for deploying, developing, and managing Workers, KV, R2, D1, Vectorize, Hyperdrive, Workers AI, Containers, Queues, Workflows, Pipelines, and Secrets Store. Load before running wrangler commands to ensure correct syntax and best practices. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop

commands.name: schedule

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

Load when writing new Workers, reviewing Worker code, configuring wrangler.jsonc, or checking for common Workers anti-patterns (streaming, floating promises, global state, secrets, bindings, observability). Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.

commands.name: cloudflare:wrangler
commands.description: (cloudflare) Cloudflare Workers CLI for deploying, developing, and managing Workers, KV, R2, D1, Vectorize, Hyperdrive, Workers AI, Containers, Queues, Workflows, Pipelines, and Secrets Store. Load before running wrangler commands to ensure correct syntax and best practices. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: api-db-go-endpoints
commands.description: Full endpoint catalog for api-db-go - every route with its path/query/body params, required fields, and expected status codes, grouped by domain. Use when you need to know which endpoint to call, what parameters it takes, or what it returns. commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

1	package validations
2	
3	import (
4		"kena.bot/api-db-go/internal/domain/dbguild"
5	)
6	
7	// UpdateModuleModerationBody mirrors the Node `updateModuleModerationSchema`
8	// (a `.strict()` object of `.optional()` fields). The handler decodes this
9	// with `DisallowUnknownFields` (matching the zod `.strict()` — unknown
10	// keys top-level OR nested are a 400) and then re-decodes the SAME raw
11	// body as `map[string]any`, which the repository merges into the existing
12	// subdoc via `mongo.MergeDeepJSON` by KEY PRESENCE: a key absent in the
13	// body is left alone; an explicit `false`/`0`/`""`/`null` is applied and
14	// overrides the stored value; nested objects (`commands_global`, `mute`,
15	// `automod`) recurse; the `commands` map merges per-key; slices replace
16	// wholesale.
17	//
18	// UNLIKE the READ schema, the PATCH schema exposes NO `schema_version`
19	// / `updated_at` — those are stamped by the repo on every write. Every
20	// other READ field IS patchable here (the READ and PATCH catalogs
21	// otherwise match).
22	//
23	// `log_channel_id` is the only TOP-LEVEL nullable string (`string |
24	// null`). Because merge is presence-based, sending `null` clears it to
25	// null and omitting the key preserves the stored value — exactly like
26	// Node's `mergeDeep`, with no special-case handling in this struct. The
27	// nested nullables (`mute.role_id`, each command's `dm_embed.color`)
28	// ride inside their parent structs and are merged recursively.
29	//
30	// REMAINING CAVEATS (inherited from the old MergeDeep mold, NOT from
31	// presence-based behaviour):
32	//   - Go's json decoder does NOT enforce zod's REQUIRED-ness inside a
33	//     present nested object (Node's `commandAccessUpdateSchema` /
34	//     `automod*` rule schemas are `.strict()` with every field
35	//     required), so a partial nested object that Node would 400 is
36	//     accepted here and the missing leaves stay zero — the same
37	//     non-strict-required behaviour every Go module body has.
38	//   - The zod value constraints (`dm_embed.content` max 4000) are NOT
39	//     enforced here. Same as every other Go module body.
40	//
41	// Cada clave de nivel superior del schema DEBE tener su puntero aquí: si falta
42	// una, el PATCH de la dashboard se come un 400 "unknown field" (el handler
43	// decodifica con `DisallowUnknownFields`). Por eso los siete bloques del v3
44	// (`protection`, `escalation`, `effects`, `raid`, `gate`, `antinuke`,
45	// `lockdown`) están listados igual que `automod` — y `flows` (v4) igual.
46	//
47	// `Flows` reutiliza `dbguild.ModerationFlow` TAL CUAL (mismo precedente que
48	// `Creators *[]dbguild.TempvoiceCreator` / `TicketTypes *[]dbguild.TicketsType`
49	// / `TicketTypes *[]dbguild.ModmailTicketType`), no un tipo "Body" duplicado:
50	// el struct de dominio YA tiene exactamente la forma que la dashboard envía
51	// (§5.3 del contrato de flujos: el PATCH sustituye el array ENTERO, así que
52	// cada flujo llega completo, con `id`/`created_at`/`updated_at` incluidos).
53	// Los `params` de trigger/condiciones/pasos siguen siendo `map[string]any`
54	// libre — su forma la valida el catálogo compartido, no Go — así que
55	// `DisallowUnknownFields` no los toca; sí rechaza cualquier clave desconocida
56	// a nivel de `ModerationFlow`/`ModerationFlowScope`/etc., que es justo lo que
57	// se quiere.
58	type UpdateModuleModerationBody struct {
59		Enabled            *bool                                 `json:"enabled,omitempty"`
60		CommandMode        *dbguild.ModerationCommandMode        `json:"command_mode,omitempty"`
61		CommandsGlobal     *dbguild.ModerationCommandAccess      `json:"commands_global,omitempty"`
62		Commands           *map[string]dbguild.ModerationCommand `json:"commands,omitempty"`
63		Mute               *dbguild.ModerationMute               `json:"mute,omitempty"`
64		LogChannelID       *string                               `json:"log_channel_id,omitempty"`
65		TrackNativeActions *bool                                 `json:"track_native_actions,omitempty"`
66		Automod            *dbguild.ModerationAutomod            `json:"automod,omitempty"`
67		Protection         *dbguild.ModerationProtection         `json:"protection,omitempty"`
68		Escalation         *dbguild.ModerationEscalation         `json:"escalation,omitempty"`
69		Effects            *dbguild.ModerationEffects            `json:"effects,omitempty"`
70		Raid               *dbguild.ModerationRaid               `json:"raid,omitempty"`
71		Gate               *dbguild.ModerationGate               `json:"gate,omitempty"`
72		Antinuke           *dbguild.ModerationAntinuke           `json:"antinuke,omitempty"`
73		Lockdown           *dbguild.ModerationLockdown           `json:"lockdown,omitempty"`
74		Flows              *[]dbguild.ModerationFlow             `json:"flows,omitempty"`
75	}
76

490		WindowMs   int                               `bson:"window_ms"  json:"window_ms"`
491		Punishment ModerationNukePunishmentOrInherit `bson:"punishment" json:"punishment"`
492	}
493	
494	// ModerationAntinuke mirrors `DBModuleModerationAntinuke` (v3) — pone un techo a
495	// las acciones destructivas por actor y unidad de tiempo. Depende del registro
496	// de auditoría (el bot necesita "Ver registro de auditoría") y, para castigar de
497	// verdad, que su rol esté POR ENCIMA del del causante. `limits` es un map igual
498	// que `commands`: clave = `ModerationNukeAction`.
499	type ModerationAntinuke struct {
500		Enabled        bool                           `bson:"enabled"          json:"enabled"`
501		Punishment     ModerationNukePunishment       `bson:"punishment"       json:"punishment"`
502		TrustedUsers   []string                       `bson:"trusted_users"    json:"trusted_users"`
503		TrustedRoles   []string                       `bson:"trusted_roles"    json:"trusted_roles"`
504		WatchBots      bool                           `bson:"watch_bots"       json:"watch_bots"`
505		AlertChannelID *string                        `bson:"alert_channel_id" json:"alert_channel_id"`
506		AlertRoleID    *string                        `bson:"alert_role_id"    json:"alert_role_id"`
507		Limits         map[string]ModerationNukeLimit `bson:"limits"           json:"limits"`
508	}
509	
510	// ModerationLockdown mirrors `DBModuleModerationLockdown` (v3) — config del
511	// bloqueo de canales (`/lock`, `/unlock` y el lockdown del anti-raid). Los
512	// mensajes vacíos caen en el texto por defecto del módulo.
513	type ModerationLockdown struct {
514		LockMessage    string   `bson:"lock_message"    json:"lock_message"`
515		UnlockMessage  string   `bson:"unlock_message"  json:"unlock_message"`
516		BypassRoles    []string `bson:"bypass_roles"    json:"bypass_roles"`
517		ServerChannels []string `bson:"server_channels" json:"server_channels"`
518	}
519	
520	// ModerationFlowTrigger es el disparador de un flujo de moderación: la clave
521	// del catálogo `MODERATION_FLOW_TRIGGER_KEYS` más sus params libres. Mismo
522	// motivo que `AutomationTrigger`: la forma de `Params` la declara el catálogo
523	// compartido de `@kena/shared/moderation-flows`, no el DB.
524	type ModerationFlowTrigger struct {
525		Type   string         `bson:"type"   json:"type"`
526		Params map[string]any `bson:"params" json:"params"`
527	}
528	
529	// ModerationFlowScope es el nodo «Scope & filters»: dónde escucha el flujo y a
530	// quién ignora. `Channels`/`Categories`/`Roles` reusan `ModerationAccessList`
531	// —el mismo mirror de `DBAccessList` que ya usa `ModerationCommandAccess`—
532	// porque viven en el mismo vertical; no se comparte entre módulos (mismo
533	// criterio que documenta `ModerationAccessMode`).
534	type ModerationFlowScope struct {
535		Channels           ModerationAccessList `bson:"channels"               json:"channels"`
536		Categories         ModerationAccessList `bson:"categories"             json:"categories"`
537		Roles              ModerationAccessList `bson:"roles"                  json:"roles"`
538		IgnoreBots         bool                 `bson:"ignore_bots"            json:"ignore_bots"`
539		IgnoreAdmins       bool                 `bson:"ignore_admins"          json:"ignore_admins"`
540		CooldownSeconds    int                  `bson:"cooldown_seconds"       json:"cooldown_seconds"`
541		RateLimitPerMinute int                  `bson:"rate_limit_per_minute"  json:"rate_limit_per_minute"`
542	}
543	
544	// ModerationFlowCondition es una condición de una rama (la raíz o una
545	// alternativa). `Negate` es el interruptor «no». `Params` va SIN TIPAR a
546	// propósito, igual que `AutomationCondition`: su forma la declara el catálogo
547	// de `@kena/shared/moderation-flows`.
548	type ModerationFlowCondition struct {
549		ID     string         `bson:"id"     json:"id"`
550		Type   string         `bson:"type"   json:"type"`
551		Negate bool           `bson:"negate" json:"negate"`
552		Params map[string]any `bson:"params" json:"params"`
553	}
554	
555	// ModerationFlowStep es un paso: una acción de moderación, `set_variable`,
556	// `wait` o `stop`. Se reutiliza tanto para `setup` como para los `steps` de
557	// cada rama.
558	type ModerationFlowStep struct {
559		ID     string         `bson:"id"     json:"id"`
560		Type   string         `bson:"type"   json:"type"`
561		Params map[string]any `bson:"params" json:"params"`
562	}
563	
564	// ModerationFlowBranch es una rama alternativa «else if» / «else»: sin
565	// condiciones es el «si no» final y debe ir última (lo valida el catálogo
566	// compartido, no el DB).
567	type ModerationFlowBranch struct {
568		ID            string                    `bson:"id"             json:"id"`
569		ConditionMode string                    `bson:"condition_mode" json:"condition_mode"`
570		Conditions    []ModerationFlowCondition `bson:"conditions"     json:"conditions"`
571		Steps         []ModerationFlowStep      `bson:"steps"          json:"steps"`
572	}
573	
574	// ModerationFlow es un flujo de moderación completo: Trigger → Scope &
575	// filters → Setup → If (condiciones raíz) → then/else. Espejo de
576	// `DBModerationFlow` (§1 del contrato de flujos), MISMO orden de campos.
577	//
578	// `Branches` lleva `omitempty` (bson Y json) a propósito — único campo de
579	// colección de este struct que lo lleva: "ausente o vacío = sin ramas" es un
580	// estado legítimo (ver el comentario del campo), igual que `Automation.Branches`
581	// en `module_automation.go`. El resto de colecciones (`Setup`, `Conditions`,
582	// `Steps`) NUNCA omitempty: una lista vacía tiene que serializar `[]`.
583	type ModerationFlow struct {
584		// ID es un `crypto.randomUUID()` estable de por vida — va en la URL del
585		// editor de la dashboard.
586		ID      string                `bson:"id"      json:"id"`
587		Name    string                `bson:"name"    json:"name"`
588		Enabled bool                  `bson:"enabled" json:"enabled"`
589		Trigger ModerationFlowTrigger `bson:"trigger" json:"trigger"`
590		Scope   ModerationFlowScope   `bson:"scope"   json:"scope"`
591		// Setup son los pasos previos a la bifurcación (típicamente `set_variable`).
592		Setup         []ModerationFlowStep `bson:"setup"          json:"setup"`
593		ConditionMode string               `bson:"condition_mode" json:"condition_mode"`
594		// Conditions son las condiciones de la rama RAÍZ (el «If» del editor).
595		// Vacío = siempre pasa.
596		Conditions []ModerationFlowCondition `bson:"conditions" json:"conditions"`
597		// Steps son los pasos de la rama raíz (el `then`).
598		Steps    []ModerationFlowStep   `bson:"steps"    json:"steps"`
599		Branches []ModerationFlowBranch `bson:"branches,omitempty" json:"branches,omitempty"`
600		// DebugUntil: hasta cuándo se persiste CADA bloqueo como fila propia en
601		// `moderation.flow_run_blocks` (ISO-8601). `nil` o pasado = sólo contadores
602		// agregados. Es el botón «Debug 15 min» del editor.
603		DebugUntil *string `bson:"debug_until" json:"debug_until"`
604		CreatedAt  string  `bson:"created_at"  json:"created_at"`
605		UpdatedAt  string  `bson:"updated_at"  json:"updated_at"`
606	}
607	
608	// ModuleModeration matches `DBModuleModeration`. Field order follows
609	// `moduleModerationSchema`. Like greeter/tempvoice/giveaway it carries a
610	// per-module `updated_at` that the repo stamps to `now` on every write.
611	type ModuleModeration struct {
612		SchemaVersion int  `bson:"schema_version"       json:"schema_version"`
613		Enabled       bool `bson:"enabled"              json:"enabled"`
614		// EnabledSince es la fecha de la PRIMERA activación del módulo en este
615		// guild — WRITE-ONCE: se estampa al activar por primera vez y no se
616		// reescribe nunca (ni al desactivar ni al reactivar). Sostiene el
617		// derecho legacy: un guild que activó moderation antes del corte de
618		// `globals.module_premium_cutoffs` conserva el módulo entero gratis.
619		// `nil` (campo ausente en Mongo) = nunca activado.
620		EnabledSince       *JSONDate                    `bson:"enabled_since,omitempty" json:"enabled_since"`
621		CommandMode        ModerationCommandMode        `bson:"command_mode"         json:"command_mode"`
622		CommandsGlobal     ModerationCommandAccess      `bson:"commands_global"      json:"commands_global"`
623		Commands           map[string]ModerationCommand `bson:"commands"             json:"commands"`
624		Mute               ModerationMute               `bson:"mute"                 json:"mute"`
625		LogChannelID       *string                      `bson:"log_channel_id"       json:"log_channel_id"`
626		TrackNativeActions bool                         `bson:"track_native_actions" json:"track_native_actions"`
627		Automod            ModerationAutomod            `bson:"automod"              json:"automod"`
628		Protection         ModerationProtection         `bson:"protection"           json:"protection"`
629		Escalation         ModerationEscalation         `bson:"escalation"           json:"escalation"`
630		Effects            ModerationEffects            `bson:"effects"              json:"effects"`
631		Raid               ModerationRaid               `bson:"raid"                 json:"raid"`
632		Gate               ModerationGate               `bson:"gate"                 json:"gate"`
633		Antinuke           ModerationAntinuke           `bson:"antinuke"             json:"antinuke"`
634		Lockdown           ModerationLockdown           `bson:"lockdown"             json:"lockdown"`
635		// Flows son los flujos de moderación configurables desde el constructor
636		// visual (v4). NUNCA `omitempty`: una lista vacía serializa `[]`, jamás
637		// `null` — mismo criterio que `Automations`.
638		Flows     []ModerationFlow `bson:"flows"                json:"flows"`
639		UpdatedAt JSONDate         `bson:"updated_at"           json:"updated_at"`
640	}
641	
642	// ── Defaults ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
643	
644	// AutomodDefaultTimeoutMs es la duración por defecto del tempmute (5 minutos)
645	// que se aplica cuando la acción de una regla es `delete_timeout`.

3	// UpdateModuleAutomationBody es el cuerpo del PATCH del módulo de
4	// automatizaciones. El handler lo decodifica con `DisallowUnknownFields` (el
5	// equivalente del `.strict()` de zod: una clave desconocida es un 400) y luego
6	// vuelve a decodificar el MISMO cuerpo crudo como `map[string]any`, que es lo
7	// que el repositorio mezcla con `mongo.MergeDeepJSON` por PRESENCIA de clave.
8	//
9	// Igual que en el resto de módulos, el PATCH NO expone `schema_version` ni
10	// `updated_at`: los estampa el repositorio en cada escritura. `enabled_since`
11	// tampoco, porque es WRITE-ONCE del servidor.
12	//
13	// AVISO sobre `automations`: el merge SUSTITUYE los arrays enteros, no los
14	// fusiona. Es justo lo que hace falta —así se puede BORRAR una automatización
15	// mandando la lista sin ella—, pero implica que quien escriba tiene que enviar
16	// la lista COMPLETA. Un PATCH con una sola automatización borra las demás.
17	//
18	// La forma de cada automatización NO se valida aquí. Quien la valida es el
19	// catálogo compartido (`@kena/shared/automation`) en las dos puntas: la
20	// dashboard antes de dejar publicar y el módulo antes de ejecutar. Repetir esas
21	// reglas en Go sería una tercera copia que se separaría de las otras dos, y la
22	// que peor se detecta: el documento se guardaría igual.
23	type UpdateModuleAutomationBody struct {
24		Enabled          *bool             `json:"enabled,omitempty"`
25		Automations      *[]map[string]any `json:"automations,omitempty"`
26		LogChannelID     *string           `json:"log_channel_id,omitempty"`
27		MaxActionsPerRun *int              `json:"max_actions_per_run,omitempty"`
28	}
